children.text: The problem

Every new service asks for an email address. Use your main one and the inbox fills up while your trail spreads everywhere. Use a third-party alias service and the address is not really yours — if they shut down, it goes with them.
What I built

Persistent email aliases on your own domain, running entirely on Cloudflare. Create as many addresses as you need, have them all land in one inbox, and because the domain is yours, the addresses last as long as the domain does.
How it works

Cloudflare Email Routing receives the mail, a Worker processes it, D1 stores the alias mapping, and R2 holds attachments. React on the front, Hono for the API, TypeScript throughout. No server to maintain.
Open source, and 27 stars on GitHub so far.

data.title: R2, meet Finder.
data.summary: Cloud storage that behaves like a local folder.

children.text: The problem
Cloudflare R2 is cheap and fast, but using it from macOS usually means macFUSE — which demands a kernel extension, security approvals, and a reboot.
What I built
A POSIX file system on top of R2, mounted in Finder over SMB. No macFUSE, no kernel extension, no reboot.
How it works
JuiceFS provides the POSIX layer over R2 objects, Redis holds the metadata, and Samba inside Docker exposes the result as an ordinary network share that Finder picks up directly.
The outcome is an object bucket that looks and behaves like a folder in the Finder sidebar.

data.title: A little signal from your AI.
data.summary: A notification when your agent finishes.

children.text: The problem
An agent running a long task leaves you waiting without knowing when it ends, so the terminal keeps pulling your attention back.
What I built
A DeepSeek Harness plugin that gives the agent a tool to notify you itself when a task completes — to ntfy, or to any webhook.
Small, but it changes how you work: long tasks can be left alone, and the notice comes to you.

data.title: Mutiarapc

children.text: The problem
A private tutoring business ran scheduling, attendance, tutor pay, and invoicing on manual records. Every schedule change meant copying it out again, and every invoice meant recalculating.
What I built
A mobile-first platform that runs the whole operation in one place, from class scheduling to invoices.

data.title: LamboServer
data.summary: Managing a local dev environment without touching the terminal.

children.text: The problem
Starting and stopping Nginx, MySQL, PHP, and PostgreSQL on macOS means remembering a different command for each service, and checking them one by one when something is not running.
What I built
A native macOS desktop app that starts, stops, and monitors all of those services from one place.
The interesting decision
The core is a unified service registry in Go. Every service is driven through the same interface, so adding a new one never touches the core logic.
Shipped as a self-contained
.dmg
installer with a guided first run, so it works without manual configuration.
Built with Go, TypeScript, React, and Wails v2.

data.title: Fakepace
data.summary: Draw a running route, set the pace, export it as TCX.

children.text: Where it came from
It started as a joke on Threads about people paying someone else to fill in their Strava. If that market exists, the tool may as well exist too.
What it does
Fakepace lets you draw a route on a map, set pace and elevation, add simulated heart rate, then download a TCX file ready to upload to Strava or Garmin Connect.
The interesting parts to build
Routes that snap to real roads.
A drawn line is fitted to actual streets rather than straight segments between points.
Pace and elevation that hold up.
The generated numbers have to stay consistent across the route, including on climbs.
TCX that platforms accept.
The format is fussy; a file that drifts slightly gets rejected.
Status
A live, paid product starting at IDR 5,000 per file, with its own guides and articles. The traffic is real.

data.title: OpenWrt for the Orange Pi Zero 3
data.summary: Fixing Wi-Fi that would not register, then writing the theme too.

children.text: The problem
The Orange Pi Zero 3 uses a Unisoc UWE5622 (AW859A) Wi-Fi chip, whose OpenWrt support is not mature. On the images going around, the radio comes up but the LuCI Wi-Fi page stays empty.
What I did
A driver and firmware for the UWE5622, plus a device tree patch so the board is described correctly.
An implementation of
.dump_station
, the piece that lets LuCI ask the driver for client status so the Wi-Fi page finally fills in.
luci-theme-opizwrt
, a LuCI theme with a real dark mode and its own login page.
Why it is public
Debugging at this level costs a full build, flash, and boot cycle per guess. Both repositories are open source so the next person with the same board does not have to repeat it.

data.title: The Wi-Fi that would not show up
data.summary: Building my own OpenWrt image because someone else's build hid the Wi-Fi.

children.text: I was running OpenWrt on an Orange Pi Zero 3 using an image someone else had built. Everything worked except one thing: the Wi-Fi page in LuCI was empty. The hardware was there, but the interface would not show it.
Finding where it broke

The board's Wi-Fi chip is a Unisoc UWE5622 (AW859A) — not a chip with mature OpenWrt support. The problem turned out to be layered: the driver, the firmware, and a device tree that did not describe the hardware correctly.
The specific reason the LuCI page stayed empty was
.dump_station
. Without that implementation, LuCI has no way to ask the driver about client status, so the Wi-Fi page has nothing to render even while the radio is up.
The process was tedious
Debugging at this level means building an image, flashing it, booting the board, looking at the result, and starting over. There is no shortcut — every guess costs a full cycle.
What came out
A driver, firmware, and device tree patch that make the Wi-Fi work, plus a
.dump_station
implementation so the LuCI Wi-Fi page finally fills in. All of it is on GitHub, so the next person with the same board does not have to repeat the same cycle.
And since I was already in there, I built my own LuCI theme.

data.title: Every service wants an email, and my inbox pays for it
data.summary: A small frustration that turned into Mailriz.

children.text: Every time I sign up for something new, I am asked for an email address. I hand over the same one, and slowly my inbox fills with things I never asked for.
Why aliases

If every service gets its own address, two things immediately improve. Spam becomes traceable — if an address I only ever used in one place suddenly gets busy, I know exactly who leaked it. And that address can be switched off without disturbing anything else.
Why not an existing service
Third-party alias services solve the problem but move the dependency. The addresses live on their domain. If the service shuts down or changes its pricing, every address goes with it.
If the aliases are on your own domain, they last as long as the domain does.
What I ended up building
Mailriz: unlimited aliases on your own domain, all landing in one inbox, running entirely on Cloudflare with no server to maintain.
I shared it thinking it was only my problem. It turned out plenty of people felt the same.

data.title: A small server on my desk
data.summary: Why I run Proxmox at home.

children.text: In the corner of my desk there is an untidy pile: one machine running Proxmox, a few small boards, loose hard drives, and more cables than I remember owning.
Why bother

The cloud makes almost everything easy, and that is exactly the problem when the goal is to learn. When a provider handles networking, storage, and recovery for you, you never really meet the parts that can break.
A homelab reverses that. Nobody handles anything for you.
What I got out of it
A lot of what I now do at work I met here first — virtualisation, networking, storage, and the habit of proving something can be restored before calling it done.
As a bonus, it is the safest place to break things.
